scope: Recovery dedicated-daemon consumers, service restoration and disposable native fault orchestration

historical_findings.observed: Different journal operations could share a daemon without a daemon-wide lock, allowing one barrier to kill another restoration.
Unguarded repair or malformed journal arrays could abort before known resource and service cleanup.
Any nonzero rival exit could count as lock rejection; dedicated service scope import and retained-corruption retries also required correction.

corrective_observations: Daily, standalone, restoration and PostgreSQL entry points hold the same private provision-base flock across execution and cleanup; nested reuse is PID-bound and an actual fork regression rejects bypass.
Malformed current and retained creator authority prohibit daemon restart; known safe cleanup remains independent.
The fault owner has durable pre-exec fork ownership and exact pidfd exit proof before daemon restart.
Rival concurrency requires exit 73 and the exact structured run_lock_contended marker.
Dedicated service context restoration uses its own endpoint; shared staging service restoration retains the original endpoint and cannot be cleared by a disposable daemon proof.
